key_gap: Both sides solve the same two subgames from the verified payoff matrix — without the system, backward induction gives (enter, accommodate) = (6, 5) and the bare fight threat is non-credible (3 < 6); with the sunk, observable system (cost 2, fight-only +4), fight = 5 > accommodate = 4, deterrence becomes credible, Z stays out and L nets 10 — and both select 'buy the system' (NPV +4). The gap is execution order and native language: the human's first move is the game form (players/strategies/payoffs verified before any alternatives), and the sunkness check is the load-bearing insight delivered first-class ('if the system were resellable, accommodate 8 > fight 7 and deterrence collapses — it is not the technology that deters Z; it is L's inability to resell it'), while the AI screened a partnership alternative the closed payoff data could not support, then recovered the identical equilibrium with scaffolding and reached the sunkness point as a verification step rather than the central mechanism.
learning_signal: For commitment problems, the game form is the first move: enumerate players, strategies, and verified payoffs, then solve by backward induction in the base game and re-solve after each proposed commitment move; the load-bearing test is the binding property — an irreversible, observable, use-conditioned cost is what changes the opponent's calculus, so check explicitly that a recoverable or hidden version of the same move would collapse the equilibrium (resellable system: accommodate 8 > fight 7 → deterrence fails); conclude with the expected play (abandonment + niche monitoring) and the NPV of the commitment vs the next-best alternative, and name the assumptions (complete information, verified effect, observability) that the conclusion requires.
suggested_improvement: Add to WHAT/WHY for competitive investment decisions: (a) if a closed payoff model is supplied, start with the game form — players, strategies, payoff matrix — before generating alternatives; (b) solve the base subgame by backward induction and explicitly record any non-credible-threat case (the 'we will fight' cheap-talk trap); (c) for each proposed commitment move, re-solve the entry subgame after the move and run the sunkness/observability check (would a resellable or unobserved version of the move fail to change the equilibrium? if yes, the commitment is load-bearing and must be the headline of the recommendation); (d) discard alternatives that the closed payoff data cannot price at screening rather than costing a pass; (e) emit expected play + NPV, not just a yes/no.

key_gap: The pure strategic play produced the model's prediction — offer reservation + ε, all couriers accept, book $3.1M — and treated the 2024 pilot's 41% walk-off (at a smaller cut) as noise, exactly the registered weakness (payoff assumptions fragile): utility = money only, atomized couriers, fixed outside options, acceptance p = 1 by construction. The AI treated the model's prediction as a claim and confronted it with the case's own verified field data: the pilot implies p(accept | ε-offer) ≈ 0.6, so EV(ε-offer) ≈ 0.6·3.1 − 0.4·1.9 ≈ 1.1 < EV(fairness-premium offer) ≈ 0.97·2.2 ≈ 2.13, and the ε-offer only wins at p ≳ 0.85 — far above the field estimate — so the decision flipped from approve to a pilot-gated plan (pilot first, scale only at p ≥ 0.85, else premium).
learning_signal: When an equilibrium prediction rests on utility assumptions (money-only, atomized, one-shot), the model output is a bound, not a forecast: enumerate the fragile assumptions and confront each against the field data in the same brief — here the chat group contradicts atomization, 34% multi-app churn contradicts fixed outside options, and the 2024 pilot falsifies p = 1 (41% walk-off at a smaller cut than proposed). Price the decision-relevant parameter (acceptance probability) from that field data, recompute EV across offer designs (ε-offer ≈ 1.1 vs premium ≈ 2.13), find the break-even (p ≳ 0.85) to show how much the verdict depends on the assumption, and embed a cheap probe (one-district pilot) as a gate so the scale decision runs on measured p, not assumed p.
suggested_improvement: Add to WHY a 'model-vs-data confrontation' step for strategic decisions: (a) before accepting a prediction, list the behavior/utility assumptions it depends on (money-only utility, atomization, fixed outside options, one-shot, p = 1); (b) search the supplied evidence for direct contradictions — prior pilots, coordination artifacts, churn data — and estimate the decision-relevant parameter from that data; (c) recompute EV with field parameter values and state the break-even value at which the verdict flips; (d) if the verdict flips under field values, recommend the cheaper of pilot-then-scale or the robust offer, with an explicit pass/fail threshold for the pilot; (e) elevate any assumption the equilibrium needs but the data contradicts to the headline risk of the decision packet.
